title: How the Claude Code team does code review
titleZh: Claude Code 团队如何进行代码审查
author: pretext
relevanceReason: 命中 4 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: We've said before that Claude writes about 90 percent of Claude Code's own code. So how do we review code at the volume we produce it? Does anyone read code anymore? And if something breaks, who catches it? This post covers the code review flow on the Claude Code team and how it has evolved. From June to September, merged pull requests to Claude Code's codebase more than doubled while the share that had to be reverted fell by more than 40 percent. We didn't remove review. But we did move most of the reading to machines, optimized for human time and attention, and invested heavily in making it fast and easy to undo mistakes. RETHINKING THE PURPOSE OF CODE REVIEW When agents write code, the number of changes goes up, fast. In Anthropic's monorepo, changes landing per day went from about 2,500 in May to more than 30,000 in September this year. Claude Code lives in its own repository, separate from the monorepo, but it's seeing a lot of pressure too. When you are shipping this fast, manual, line-by-line code review is incredibly difficult if not impossible. Code review does two jobs:
Find and fix issues before they ship Build shared context and codebase understanding across the team

This article mainly focuses on finding and fixing issues, but we will come back to the second job near the end. We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?" Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague. Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny. THE SCARCE RESOURCE: HUMAN TIME AND ATTENTION We want to preserve human time and attention for issues only humans can solve and make sure automated checks catch the rest. At our current rate of change, there is still an incredible amount of work for humans to do, and our team encounters new and novel challenges almost daily. Human time covers both sides of review's cost: the time people spend reviewing, and the time they spend fixing what bad code breaks. Cutting the first doesn't help if the time just shows up in the second. So the goal is that most pull requests in the Claude Code repos (the CLI, the desktop and web apps, and the mobile apps) merge with at most one human in the loop, who can be the author, with no increase in reverts or incidents. To measure human time, we track human approvals per PR (median and 95th percentile), human comments, and how long a PR waits on a person. Revert and incident rates are the guardrail: if they rise, we haven't saved human time, we've only moved it. THE LIFE OF A CHANGE A typical change, from an engineer's laptop (or a Claude session in Slack), goes through multiple layers of code review. The life of a changeA typical Claude Code change, from the author's machine to usersFIG AMost of the path is automated; a person's attention goes where the risk is LAYER BY LAYER Layers, not one gateSix layers of checks, with rollback under themFIG BEach layer catches some problems and misses others. Few get through all of them, and rollback handles the rest. 1. The work is verified before anyone else looks Most review now happens before a PR exists. We give Claude something it can run—like tests, a build or a screenshot to compare against the design—and ask it to show the output instead of saying it's done. Then a subagent reviews the diff with fresh context. Both habits come from our best-practices guide. Before opening a PR, many of us also run a few internal skills: one hunts for bugs, one simplifies the diff, and one checks the behavior end to end. UI changes also get checked against our design guidelines. Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, has called giving Claude a way to verify its work probably the most important thing for getting good results. He estimates it makes the final result two to three times better, and writes, "Verification looks different for each domain. It might be as simple as running a bash command, or running a test suite, or testing the app in a browser or phone simulator." When the automated reviewer keeps flagging the same thing, we fix it at the source: in the skill, with a lint rule, or with updates to instructional files such as:

CLAUDE.md tells Claude what the project is: the stack, the conventions, the goals and the non-goals. Every review loads it, so in a large codebase we keep it short and point to other docs from there. The reviewer also flags code that breaks a convention in it, and changes that make a line in it out of date. REVIEW.md, written by code owners, tells the reviewer what matters in their part of the code. We check separately whether the reviewer actually follows it. The good ones are short. They say what failure looks like in that repo (for docs it's "it lies," for config it's "it misroutes"), cap the nits, list paths to skip, and ask for a file and line as evidence instead of a guess from a name. They also ask for a summary that starts with a count and says plainly when there's nothing to fix.

2. AI review on every pull request Every pull request gets a Claude review before a person looks. It reads the diff against the whole repo and the PR's stated intent, and asks: does the change solve its problem, fit the system, or break something else? On a bug fix, it looks for the root cause. The public version, Code Review for Claude Code, is now generally available on Team and Enterprise plans, and /code-review runs a lighter version locally. When we launched the research preview, the share of internal PRs getting substantive review comments went from 16% to 54%. Most PRs over 1,000 lines get findings, and most small ones come back clean. Admins set each repo to Quick, Standard, or Deep. Deep is worth it where one missed bug costs more than the extra review time. Findings get verified by other agents before humans review them. Several agents look for bugs at the same time. Then a separate group votes on each finding, and it only gets posted if enough of them agree it's real. Findings that are only about style, diagnostics, or cleanup get dropped. We A/B tested those filters on our own PRs before keeping them. What's left shows up as inline comments sorted by severity. Each is tagged Important, Nit, or Pre-existing, so a bug the PR didn't introduce doesn't look like the author's fault. Every finding has to be answered. You either fix it or resolve the thread with a reason. Often an agent picks up the fix overnight, so the author comes back to a PR that's already been through another round. 3. Security review that can block Security gets its own automated review too. A PR can't merge while any finding from the bug review or the security review is still open. You either fix it or close the thread with a short reason, which is how you clear a false positive. If a later commit fixes the issue, the finding clears on its own. You can set up the same thing with the open-source security review GitHub Action or the /security-review command. Setup is covered in automated security reviews in Claude Code. 4. Automated checks that block The usual: lint, type checks, tests on every platform, and a build. (We wrote about scaling CI for this volume here.) A typical CLI pull request may run dozens of checks before anyone looks at it. The PR template asks how the change was tested and how to undo it. Claude can fill that in, but the person who asked for the change signs off on it. 5. Human approval, scaled by risk A docs fix and an auto-updater change carry different risk, so they get different review. RiskExamplesHuman approvalsLowDocs, copy, internal-only features, additive changes behind a flagNone required once automated review and security checks are greenMediumOrdinary product changes, and changes to sensitive areas such as caching, the auto-updater, or system promptsOne personHighThe highest-risk code, plus a small set of paths that always need two peopleTwo people The change sets the tier, not the author. A classifier reads the change and picks its risk tier. A second classifier asks whether this particular change needs another person even when its tier says it doesn't. Some paths always need a person, anything owners have listed as sensitive and any CI workflow file. Only trusted authors get the lighter paths. Only authors on the repo's trusted list get the lighter paths, mostly the team that owns it. Everyone else needs a second person to approve. An agent's approval never counts as a person's, either. Automated review can clear a low-risk change, but it can't fill a slot that calls for a human. Whoever prompted the change is on the hook for it. On an agent-written PR, the person directing the agent counts as one of the required reviewers, the same as if they'd typed the code themselves. An approval covers one specific commit. If new commits land that the system can't vouch for, like an agent's push or a merge someone resolved by hand, the approval has to be given again. 6. Merge queue, flags and a gradual release The merge queue re-runs every check against main with the change applied, so two PRs that pass separately can't combine into a broken main. New behavior usually ships behind a flag to Anthropic employees first, and our heavy use often surfaces regressions before users do. Public releases go to the latest channel first. The stable channel trails it. 7. Fast detection, fast rollback Some mistakes will still get through, so the last layer is about catching them fast. Flags turn off without a deploy. Claude Code has a weekly on-call rotation, and incident reviews ask which layer should have caught the issue. Noticing a bad merge still depends on the author and on-call as well as the revert and incident dashboards. We don't yet have circuit breakers that tighten approval when those numbers move; engineers here want them before more code moves to zero-human merges. One colleague said slowing down does lower your error rate, but mostly because you're doing less of everything. We'd rather get faster at noticing and fixing problems. HOW WE MAKE THE REVIEWER BETTER Our code review process is constantly improving in a loop. Any incidents are now an eval. The team collected past PRs that caused incidents, with their fix-forwards and reverts, and had engineers who know that code confirm each bug and where it lived. The reviewer runs against that set daily. Our incidents are the evalBuilt from past incidents and reverts, run every dayFIG CThe eval grows with every incident, and every change to the reviewer is scored against all of it. We measure noise by watching what people do with the comments. It's easy to catch more bugs if you don't mind flagging a lot of non-bugs, so we need a check on that. We sort every comment the reviewer leaves by how the person on the PR responded: they fixed it, said it was wrong, said the behavior was intentional, or decided it didn't matter. We also run the reviewer on PRs we know are clean and count how often it reports something that would have led someone to make a harmful change. Our priority, written down, is catching real bugs first and cutting review rounds second. Noise costs more when the author is an agent. A person can wave off a nit in seconds. An agent fixes it, which means another commit and another round of review. Review has to converge. An agent author and an agent reviewer can keep each other busy indefinitely. One CLI PR went through more than fifty rounds of review and fixes overnight before its author stopped it. When we ran git blame on what the reviewer kept flagging, about 59% of it was code that had been there since the reviewer's first pass. The reviewer was rarely finding new bugs, it was finding a few more old ones each round. We made it worse ourselves. We'd gotten used to running several rounds by default, since each pass catches something new. This can be worthwhile on a risky change, but not on every PR. comments.author: avinoth
comments.textRawHtml:
This is like one of Google’s infrastructure blog. Google scale things are only relevant and appropriate for them. We had lots of bitter lessons from smaller engineering teams following the process with the justification that “this is how Google does it”.

Similarly, Anthropic can afford to do this because they have virtually unlimited tokens and labs to train models for their specific usecase. The rest of us need code comprehension lest we become dependent on continuous supply of tokens (which is a state these labs badly want to achieve)

So, unless you work at a lab, or have unlimited tokens guaranteed through the life of your company, it would do both the company and you good to continue to read the code and not let these 30k PRs per engineer be the norm.

An excerpt from the article makes my point

> Nobody on the team keeps a complete mental model of Claude Code in their head, and we don't think anyone needs to. When someone wants to understand a part of the codebase, they ask Claude to write an explainer for exactly that slice. It takes minutes and reflects the code as it is today.
comments.textZhHtml:
这就像 Google 的基础设施博客之一。谷歌规模的东西只与他们相关并且适合他们。我们从较小的工程团队那里吸取了很多惨痛的教训，他们遵循的过程是“谷歌就是这样做的”。

同样，Anthropic 也有能力做到这一点，因为他们拥有几乎无限的代币和实验室来训练针对其特定用例的模型。我们其他人需要代码理解，以免我们变得依赖于持续供应代币（这是这些实验室非常希望实现的状态）

因此，除非您在实验室工作，或者在公司的整个生命周期内保证拥有无限的代币，否则继续阅读代码而不是让每个工程师 30k PR 成为常态，对公司和您都有好处。

文章的摘录表明了我的观点

>团队成员的头脑中保留着 Claude Code 的完整心理模型，我们认为任何人都不需要这样做。当有人想要理解代码库的一部分时，他们会要求 Claude 为该部分编写一个解释器。它需要几分钟的时间并反映当前的代码。

children.author: thatsabadlook
children.textRawHtml:
Even then do we really have evidence that what they are doing is reasonable or practical for them at all? They are edging on like 3 9s uptime, what leaked of Claude code looked like soup, tons of security issues, they can't build a sandbox to save their company, and last I heard they aren't even profitable without adjusting their numbers for arbitrary things.

Think I'm good on taking advice from companies that aren't making money.
children.textZhHtml:
即便如此，我们真的有证据表明他们所做的事情对他们来说是合理的或实用的吗？他们的正常运行时间接近 3 个 9，泄露的克劳德代码看起来像汤，大量的安全问题，他们无法构建沙箱来拯救他们的公司，最后我听说，如果不调整任意事情的数字，他们甚至无法盈利。

我认为我很擅长听取不赚钱的公司的建议。

children.author: avinoth
children.textRawHtml: Exactly. What they’re doing, repeatedly, is setting a narrative that this is how software engineering should be. Always be reliant on tokens. Don’t worry about uptime or errors - agents can address it, don’t worry about security - agents can address it, don’t worry about code comprehension - agents will always be there for you.
children.textZhHtml: 正是如此。他们不断地重复着这样的故事：软件工程就应该是这样的。始终依赖代币。不用担心正常运行时间或错误 - 代理可以解决它，不用担心安全性 - 代理可以解决它，不用担心代码理解 - 代理将永远为您服务。

children.author: oblio
children.textRawHtml:
> agents will always be there for you.

In Romania an investment fund (FNI) around 2000 ran some super famous ads saying "FNI is watching" (FNI is keeping watch).

6 months later they went bankrupt.
children.textZhHtml:
> 代理商将永远为您服务。

2000 年左右，罗马尼亚的一家投资基金 (FNI) 投放了一些超级著名的广告，上面写着“FNI is Watch”（FNI 正在注视）。

6 个月后，他们破产了。

children.author: panarky
children.textRawHtml:
If they're cash-flow positive with 75% of compute going to research and training, what do you think will happen to cash flow when they shift to 50-50 training-inference?

Because "pacing the frontier" is more about flipping on the money printer switch than it is about safety.
children.textZhHtml:
如果他们的现金流为正，75% 的计算用于研究和培训，那么您认为当他们转向 50-50 训练推理时，现金流会发生什么？

因为“调整前沿”更多的是打开印钞机开关，而不是安全。

children.author: thr0w
children.textRawHtml:
> they ask Claude to write an explainer for exactly that slice

If their Claude is the same as our Claude, then this is a joke. Claude’s writing style is insidiously mind numbing. It takes constant pushing to get it to explain things in digestible English.
children.textZhHtml:
> 他们要求克劳德为那个切片写一个解释器

如果他们的克劳德和我们的克劳德一样，那么这是一个笑话。克劳德的写作风格令人心智麻木。需要不断地推动它才能用易于理解的英语解释事物。

children.author: bulbar
children.textRawHtml:
It also mixes important with unimportant information. It tends to think that a commit/bugfix is important and will happily list it together with important properties of the feature.

At least Opus 5.5 does that. Its writing is better than that if other models, though. I had other models explain stuff in an undigestable language, technically correct, but practically not what anything is about.
children.textZhHtml:
它还混合了重要和不重要的信息。它倾向于认为提交/错误修复很重要，并且很乐意将其与功能的重要属性一起列出。

至少 Opus 5.5 做到了这一点。不过，它的写作比其他模型要好。我让其他模型用难以理解的语言解释了一些东西，技术上是正确的，但实际上并不是什么内容。

children.author: elondaits
children.textRawHtml: I hate it when it realizes something that was contextually obvious to me, and then treats it like a precious nugget of wisdom, including it in the README, the comments, and the commit message. Even worse when it’s a hypothetical situation. “Even if the raw chicken is bagged and refrigerated, we want to avoid a leaky bag.”

children.author: froggy
children.textRawHtml: Try having it explain something in “ISO Plain Language standard”. It made an enormous difference for me yesterday. The language will change from dense large paragraphs to simply-worded 2-3 sentence paragraphs. I was using gpt though.
children.textZhHtml: 尝试让它解释“ISO 普通语言标准”中的某些内容。昨天这对我来说发生了巨大的变化。语言将从密集的大段落变为措辞简单的2-3句段落。不过我使用的是 gpt。

children.author: meheleventyone
children.textRawHtml: Even getting it to write less obtuse English isn't enough IMO. It seems to have real issues with structuring documentation in a way that makes it easy to follow. Also it's a real demon for leaking its context as implicit assumptions into documentation.
children.textZhHtml: 在我看来，即使让它写得不那么迟钝的英语也是不够的。以易于理解的方式构建文档似乎存在真正的问题。此外，它也是一个真正的恶魔，会将其上下文作为隐式假设泄露到文档中。

children.author: IshKebab
children.textRawHtml:
They pretty much fixed that. Plus you can influence the writing style to some extent. I tell it to use full sentences and avoid assuming I already understand the code.

Another thing is that it's very good at creating diagrams (I think someone wrote a skill for it so maybe not by default). I usually find the diagrams are even more valuable than the text.

Honestly I was skeptical but you really can just point Claude at some code and ask it to make a markdown + SVG explainer and it will do a shockingly good job.

I'd still rather read human documentation, but even before AI almost nobody writes any - especially for internal code. And they certainly don't make great diagrams.
